'''wall-lizard''' (wâl′liz″ärd), ''n.'' '''1.''' A gecko; any lizard of the family ''Gecconidæ.'' See ''Gecconidæ'' and cuts under ''gecko'' and ''Platydactylus.''—'''2.''' A common European lizard, ''Lacerta muralis.''

'''wall-net''' (wâl′net), ''n.'' A vertical net forming the wall of an inclosed space, as of a pound-net. See cut under ''pound-net.''

'''wall-newt''' (wâl′nūt), ''n.'' Same as ''wall-lizard.''
{{smaller block|The toad, the tadpole, the ''wall-newt.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 4. 135.}}}}

'''Walloon''' (wo-lön′), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< F. ''Wallon'', < OF. ''Wallon'', ''Walon'', ''Gualon'' (also ''Wallin''), < ML. ''Wallus'', L. ''Gallus'', a Gaul, Celt; cf. ''Gaul''<sup>1</sup>, ''Welsh.''] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A member of a people found chiefly in southern and southeastern Belgium, also in the neighboring parts of France, and in a few places in Rhenish Prussia near Malmedy. They are descended from the ancient Belgæ, mixed with Germanic and Roman elements.—'''2.''' In America, especially colonial New York, one of the Huguenot settlers from Artois, in northern France, etc.—'''3.''' A French dialect, spoken by the Walloons of Belgium, France, etc.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Walloons: as, the ''Walloon'' language.

'''wallop<sup>1</sup>''' (wol′op), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''walopen'', < OF. *''waloper'', ''galoper'', boil, gallop, < OFlem. ''walop'', a gallop; with an element ''-op'', perhaps orig. OFlem. ''op'', E. ''up'' (cf. the E. dial. var. ''wall-up''), < OFlem. ''wallen'' = OS. ''wallan'' = AS. ''weallan'', boil, spring forth as water does: see ''wall''<sup>2</sup>, ''well''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''gallop.''] '''1.''' To boil with a continued bubbling or heaving and rolling of the liquor, accompanied with noise. [Prov. Eng.]

See ''degeneratio'' an law, a law in regard to degeneration in n by the degeneration follows the course of th the affected fibers toward either the center c ery.—'''Wallerian method,''' the method o nerve-fibers by their degeneration at one po section at another.}}

'''wallet''' (wol′et), ''n.''   [< ME. ''walet, w'' sibly a transposition or corruption bag: see ''wattle.'' For a similar transp ''neeld'' for ''needle.'']   '''1.''' A long bag wi the middle, and space for the cont two ends: a form familiar in si purses, and revived for larger bags f use.
{{smaller block|His ''walet'' lay biforn him on his lap
{{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. t}}}}
{{smaller block|A ''Wallet'', . . . G. Bisác, i. bis saccus, a do bagge.}}
{{smaller block|As an instance of another form of the ''wal'' a very old one—may I mention the little tri of stuff, something like a bag, that is suspe hind the left shoulder of a junior barrister’s worn? . . . about eight or nine inches in le vided by a slit at the bottom into two comp of which is open and the other enclosed a holding small articles. {{right|''N. and Q.'', 7t}}}}
'''2†.''' Anything protuberant and swag pare ''wattle.''
{{smaller block|Who would believe that there were mounta Dew-lapp’d like bulls, whose throats had ha ''Wallets'' of flesh?
{{right|''Shak.'', Tem}}}}

'''3.''' A flat bag of leather, with a flap, opening with a clasp, at the top: use etc., or in a small size for carrying person.

{{smaller block|The ''wallet'', or tool-bag, is generally supp machine [bicycle or tricycle].
{{right|''Bury and Hillier'', C}}}}

'''4.''' A pocketbook, especially a lar containing papers, bank-notes laid folded, and the like.—'''5.''' A small by anglers. {{smaller|A wallet generally include needles, awl, waxed ends, shoemakers’ wa nails, coarse and fine twine, a pair of small a spring-balance to weigh fish, court-plaste nish, prepared glue, boiled linseed-oil, etc.}}

'''6.''' In ''her.'', a bearing representing a ''scrip''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Wallet open''', {{smaller|in ''her.'', a bearing scrip with the mouth open, usually having or cover turned back.}}

'''walleteer†''' (wol-e-tēr′), ''n.''   [< ''wal'' One who bears a wallet; hence, a foot; a pilgrim. ''Tollet.'' (''Jodrell.'')

'''walletful''' (wol′et-fu̇l), ''n.'' As much contains; a purseful.

{{smaller block|Wedden hure for hure welthe and wisshen That hus wyf were wex, other a ''watel-ful'' o
{{right|''Piers Plowm''}}}}

'''walleye''' (wâl′ī), ''n.''   [Early mod. E a back-formation from ''wall-eyed''.]   in a condition in which it preser no color, the iris being light-colore or opacity of the cornea being pr this condition itself.

{{smaller block|''Glauciolus'', An horse with a ''waule eye''.
{{right|''Coope''}}}} '''2.''' Divergent strabismus, in whic of the eye is conspicuous.—'''3.''' A l eye, as of some fishes.—'''4.''' A wal {{smaller|Especially—(''a'') A pike-perch (which see) wife, or wall-eyed herring. (''c'') A surf-fish, ''genteus''. [California.]}}

'''wall-eyed''' (wâl′īd), ''a.''   [Formerly ''whalle-'', ''whaule-'', ''whall-eyed'' (also separately), prob. < Icel. ''vald-eygt'' tion of ''vagl-eygr'', wall-eyed, said < ''vagl'', a disease of the eye, + ''eyg'' ''auga'', eye: see ''wall''<sup>3</sup> and ''eye''<sup>1</sup>.]   1 walleye or walleyes, as a horse.
{{smaller block|Walking would be twenty times more ge a paltry conveyance, as Blackberry was ''wa'' colt wanted a tail.
{{right|''Golds''}}}}
'''2.''' Showing much of the white having a large staring or glaring ''wall-eyed'' pike. See ''pike''<sup>2</sup>, and cut ''perch''.—'''3.''' See the quotation. [P
{{smaller block|Any work irregularly or ill done is call job. It is applied also to any very irregul}}
'''4.''' Glaring; fierce; threatening.
{{smaller block|<poem>This is . . . the vilest stro
That ever ''wall-eyed'' wrath or starin
Presented to the tears of soft rem</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Wall-eyed herring,''' the alewife or walley}}

'''wall-fern''' (wâl′fėrn), ''n.'' A small eve ''Polypodium vulgare,'' which grows walls. See ''polypody.''

'''wallflower''' (wâl′flou″ėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' An old favorite garden flower and pot-plant, ''Cheiranthus Cheiri'', native in southern Europe, where it grows on old walls, cliffs, and the sides of quarries. {{smaller|The flowers have four petals, with a spreading limb on long claws, colored a deep-orange, or in cultivation varying from pale-yellow to deep-red, are clustered in short racemes, and are sweet-scented. It is grown in many varieties, classed as single and double biennials and double perennials. It grows by preference upon walls, forming there an enduring bush, but may be planted on rocky banks, and is also one of the finest of border-plants. It formerly shared the name of ''heart’s-ease;'' and in western England a dark-red variety is called ''bleeding-heart.'' A common name also is ''gilly-flower'', or, for distinction, ''wall-gillyflower.'' The name {{img float|file=century v08 p0615 c2f1.png|width=151px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Wallflower (''Cheiranthus Cheiri'').}}}} is extended to other species of the genus and to some species of ''Erysimum''.}}

'''2.''' A man or woman who, at a ball or party, sits by the wall, or looks on without dancing, either from choice or from being unable to dance or to obtain a partner. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|I believe there are men who have shown as much self-devotion in carrying a lone ''wall-flower'' down to the supper-table as ever saint or martyr in the act that has canonized his name.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Native wallflower''' of Australia, ''Pultenæa daphnoides'', of the ''Leguminosæ''.—'''Western wallflower''' of the United States, ''Erysimum asperum'', a plant found in Ohio, and more commonly westward, with orange-yellow flowers of the size of and like those of the wallflower.}}

'''wall-fruit''' (wâl′fröt), ''n.'' Fruit which, to be ripened, must be planted against a wall.

'''wall-gecko''' (wâl′gek″ō), ''n.'' A gecko, especially ''Platydactylus muralis'' of southern Europe.

'''wall-germander''' (wâl′jėr-man″dėr), ''n.'' See ''Teucrium.''

'''wall-gillyflower''' (wâl′jil″i-flou-ėr), ''n.'' See ''wallflower.''

'''wall-grenade''' (wâl′grẹ̄-nād″), ''n.'' A bombshell somewhat larger than the hand-grenade. {{smaller|It was thrown by hand from the rampart of a fortification, or from a small mortar called a ''hand-mortar.''}}

'''wall-hawkweed''' (wâl′hâk″wēd), ''n.'' A European hawkweed, ''Hieracium murorum'', often growing on walls. Also ''French'' or ''golden lungwort.''

'''wallhick''' (wâl′hik), ''n.'' The lesser spotted woodpecker, ''Picus minor. Montagu.'' See ''hickwall.'' [Local, British.]

'''walling'''<sup>1</sup> (wâ′ling), ''n.''   [< ''wall''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Walls collectively; materials for walls.
{{smaller block|The general character of the Roman ''walling'' is described in Hartshorn’s essay “Porchester Castle.”
{{right|''C. Elton'', Origins of Eng. Hist., p. 323.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''mining'', the brick or stone lining of a shaft; steining.—{{smaller|'''Dry walling''', walling without the}} use of mortar or cement.

'''walling'''<sup>2</sup> (wâ′ling), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''wall''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'']   The act of boiling; a boiling. ''Grose.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|The ''walling'' or making of salt, &c.
{{right|''Record Soc. Lancashire and Cheshire'', XI. 114.}}}}

'''wall-ink''' (wâl′ingk), ''n.'' The brook-lime, ''Veronica Beccabunga'', a creeping plant of wet places in the northern Old World. [Scotland and Ireland: in the latter sometimes ''well-ink.'']

'''Wallis’s theorem.''' See ''theorem.''

'''wall-knot''' (wâl′not), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wale-knot.'']   ''Naut.'', a large knot made on the end of a rope by interweaving the strands in a particular manner.

'''wall-less''' (wâl′les), ''a.''   [< ''wall''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   Having no wall.
{{smaller block|The blood was poured into ''wall-less'' lacunæ.
{{right|''Huxley'', Anat. Invert., p. 283.}}}}

'''wall-lettuce''' (wâl′let″is), ''n.'' A European lettuce, ''Lactuca'' (''Prenanthes'') ''muralis.''

'''wall-light''' (wâl′līt), ''n.'' A bracket or girandole for candles or lamps.

'''wall-lizard''' (wâl′liz″ärd), ''n.'' '''1.''' A gecko; any lizard of the family ''Gecconidæ.'' See ''Gecconidæ'' and cuts under ''gecko'' and ''Platydactylus.''—'''2.''' A common European lizard, ''Lacerta muralis.''

'''wall-louse''' (wâl′lous), ''n.'' The bedbug, ''Cimex lectularius'' (''Acantha lectularia''). See cut under ''bug.''

'''wall-moss''' (wâl′môs), ''n.'' '''1.''' The yellow wall-lichen, ''Parmelia parietaria.''—'''2.''' The stonecrop or wall-pepper, ''Sedum acre.'' ''Britten and Holland.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''wall-net''' (wâl′net), ''n.'' A vertical net forming the wall of an inclosed space, as of a pound-net. See cut under ''pound-net.''

'''wall-newt''' (wâl′nūt), ''n.'' Same as ''wall-lizard.''
{{smaller block|The toad, the tadpole, the ''wall-newt.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iii. 4. 135.}}}}

'''Walloon''' (wo-lön′), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< F. ''Wallon'', < OF. ''Wallon'', ''Walon'', ''Gualon'' (also ''Wallin''), < ML. ''Wallus'', L. ''Gallus'', a Gaul, Celt; cf. ''Gaul''<sup>1</sup>, ''Welsh.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A member of a people found chiefly in southern and southeastern Belgium, also in the neighboring parts of France, and in a few places in Rhenish Prussia near Malmedy. They are descended from the ancient Belgæ, mixed with Germanic and Roman elements.—'''2.''' In America, especially colonial New York, one of the Huguenot settlers from Artois, in northern France, etc.—'''3.''' A French dialect, spoken by the Walloons of Belgium, France, etc.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Walloons: as, the ''Walloon'' language.

'''wallop<sup>1</sup>''' (wol′op), ''v. i.''   [< ME. ''walopen'', < OF. *''waloper'', ''galoper'', boil, gallop, < OFlem. ''walop'', a gallop; with an element ''-op'', perhaps orig. OFlem. ''op'', E. ''up'' (cf. the E. dial. var. ''wall-up''), < OFlem. ''wallen'' = OS. ''wallan'' = AS. ''weallan'', boil, spring forth as water does: see ''wall''<sup>2</sup>, ''well''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''gallop.'']   '''1.''' To boil with a continued bubbling or heaving and rolling of the liquor, accompanied with noise. [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|<poem>The yellow flour, bestrew’d and stir’d with haste,
Swells in the flood and thickens to a paste,
Then puffs and ''wallops'', rises to the brim,
Drinks the dry knobs that on the surface swim.</poem>
{{right|''Joel Barlow'', Hasty Pudding, i.}}}}
'''2.''' To move quickly with great but somewhat clumsy effort; gallop. See ''gallop''. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>And he anon to hym com ''waloping''.</poem>
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3325.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Swerdez swangene in two, sweltand knyghtez
Lyes wyde opyne welterande one ''walopande'' stedez.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2147.}}}}
{{smaller block|She [a seal] ''wallopped'' away with all the grace of triumph.
{{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, xxx.}}}}

'''wallop'''<sup>1</sup> (wol′op), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wallop'', ''walop'': see the verb.]   A quick motion with much agitation or effort; a gallop. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Or he wiste, he was war of the white beres,
Thei went a-wai a ''wallop'' as thei wod [mad] semed.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1770.}}}}
{{smaller block|Than the kynge rode formest hym-self a grete ''walop'', for sore hym longed to wite how the kynge Tradilyuaunt hym contened.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 233.}}}}

'''wallop'''<sup>2</sup> (wol′op), ''v. t.''   [Origin obscure; perhaps a particular use of ''wallop''<sup>1</sup>. It is appar. confused with ''wale''<sup>1</sup>, ''whale''<sup>2</sup>. There is an absurd notion that the verb is derived from the name of Sir John ''Wallop'', an ancestor of the Earl of Portsmouth, Knight of the Garter, who in Henry VIII.’s time distinguished himself by ''walloping'' the French.]   '''1.''' To castigate; beat soundly; drub; thrash. [Slang.]

{{smaller block|My father is an engineer’s labourer, and the first cause of my thieving was that he kept me without grub, and ''walloped'' me.
{{right|''Mayhew'', London Labour and London Poor, I. 468.}}}}
'''2.''' To tumble over; dash down. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.]

'''wallop<sup>2</sup>''' (wol′op), ''n.''   [< ''wallop<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.'']   A severe blow. [Slang.]

'''walloper<sup>1</sup>''' (wol′ọp-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wallop<sup>1</sup>'' + ''-er<sup>1</sup>''.]   A pot-walloper.

'''walloper<sup>2</sup>''' (wol′ọp-ėr), ''n.''   [Also ''wolloper''; < ''wallop<sup>2</sup>'' + ''-er<sup>1</sup>''.]   One who or that which wallops. [Slang.]—'''Cod-walloper,''' {{smaller|a cod-fishing vessel. [Provincetown, Massachusetts.]}}

'''walloping''' (wol′op-ing), ''a.'' Great; bouncing. [Prov. Eng. and U. S.]

'''wallow<sup>1</sup>''' (wol′ō), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''walow''; < ME. ''walowen'', ''walewen'', ''walwen'', ''welwen'', wallow, < AS. ''wealwian'', roll round, = Goth. ''walwjan'', wallow, roll, = L. ''volvere'', roll (whence ult. E. ''volute'', ''volve'', ''devolve'', etc.).]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To roll; tumble about. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Mi witte is waste nowe in wede,
I ''walowe'', I walke, nowe woo is me.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 421.}}}}
{{smaller block|He ''walweth'' and he turneth to and fro.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 229.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There saw I our great galliasses tost
Upon the ''wallowing'' waves.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Monsieur D’Olive, ii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Through the deep gulf of the chimney wide
''Wallows'' the Yule-log’s roaring tide.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Vision of Sir Launfal, ii., Prol.}}}} '''2.''' To roll the body in sand, mire, water, or other yielding substance.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
